The two talks listed in the README come with papers that describe their examples in detail. This page
rebuilds those examples with `cpt` in SQL. Every query and result below is checked by
`test/sql/cpt_talk_examples.test`, on DuckDB 1.5.6 and 2.0.

The talks' own data is not reproduced:

- The FOCuS real-data example uses AWS CloudWatch series from the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark.
  The FOCuS paper does not state the dataset's licence.
- The Hunter paper's benchmark data comes from DataStax and is not public.
- Fleming's slides have one worked example ("Linux Kernel syscall"), but it exists only as an image.

The examples here use synthetic data built to the papers' descriptions. It is generated with
`sin()`-based uniforms, so every DuckDB version and thread count produces the same series:

```sql
CREATE MACRO u(i, k) AS (abs(sin((i + 1) * 12.9898 + k * 78.233) * 43758.5453) % 1.0) * 0.999998 + 0.000001;
CREATE MACRO z(i, k) AS sqrt(-2 * ln(u(i, k))) * cos(2 * pi() * u(i, k + 1));   -- N(0, 1), Box-Muller
```

## 1. Paul Fearnhead: functional pruning and FOCuS

Talk: "Fast Online Changepoint Detection via Functional Pruning CUSUM Statistics" (University of
Edinburgh recording). Paper: Romano, Eckley, Fearnhead & Rigaill, *JMLR* 24(81), 2023,
[arXiv:2110.08205](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08205).

**What the talk is about.** FOCuS is an *online* detector. Data arrives one point at a time, and it
raises an alarm as soon as a change becomes significant. It is equivalent to running Page's CUSUM test
for every possible change size at once. The cost of every candidate change size is kept as a set of
quadratic curves, and curves that can no longer be optimal are dropped. This is *functional pruning*.
The paper shows that about log n + 1 curves survive when there is no change ("for data of size one
million, the bound on the number of quadratics is less than 15"). It reports that FOCuS processes
1 million observations in under a second.

**How it relates to cpt.** `cpt` is *offline*: it sees the whole series and finds the best segmentation.
PELT also prunes, but with an inequality on the candidate's cost (Killick et al. 2012), not by keeping
cost curves. The two answer different questions: FOCuS asks "has something changed yet?", while PELT
asks "where are the change points?". Functional pruning for the offline problem is FPOP (Maidment &
Fearnhead), which is not implemented here.

### 1a. The paper's Figure 1, offline

Figure 1 uses Gaussian data with unit variance and mean 0 before the change:

- (a) 2000 observations with a change of size 1 at 1000.
- (b) The same with a change of size 0.2.
- (c) Like (a), but with 8000 extra observations at the start, so the change comes at 9000.

The paper uses these to show CUSUM, MOSUM and Page-CUSUM failing in different ways: MOSUM loses power
on the small change in (b), and CUSUM behaves poorly on the long prefix in (c).

```sql
CREATE TABLE f1a AS SELECT list(CASE WHEN i >= 1000 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END + z(i, 1) ORDER BY i) AS xs FROM range(2000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE f1b AS SELECT list(CASE WHEN i >= 1000 THEN 0.2 ELSE 0 END + z(i, 1) ORDER BY i) AS xs FROM range(2000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE f1c AS SELECT list(CASE WHEN i >= 9000 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END + z(i, 1) ORDER BY i) AS xs FROM range(10000) t(i);

SELECT (SELECT cpt_pelt(xs, 'l2') FROM f1a), (SELECT cpt_pelt(xs, 'l2') FROM f1b), (SELECT cpt_pelt(xs, 'l2') FROM f1c);
-- [1000, 2000]   [1016, 2000]   [9000, 10000]
```

With all the data available, the long prefix in (c) costs nothing, and even the 0.2 change is found,
16 points late. How firmly it is found is a different matter. CROPS shows that it survives only for
penalties in a narrow band (the BIC value here is 2 ln 2000 ≈ 15.2):

```sql
SELECT list_transform(list_filter(cpt_crops(xs, 'l2', 5, 60), lambda e: e.n_bkps <= 2), lambda e: e.bkps) FROM f1b;
-- [[1016, 1022, 2000], [1016, 2000], [2000]]     -- [1016, 2000] for penalties ≈ 20.9 down to ≈ 7.6
```

### 1b. Detection delay

An online detector is judged by its *detection delay*: how many points after the change it raises
the alarm. Offline you can mimic this by rerunning PELT on every prefix `xs[1:t]` and asking when the
change first appears, and from when on it stays:

```sql
WITH d AS (
    SELECT name, t, len(b) > 1 AND list_bool_or(list_transform(b[1:-2], lambda e: abs(e - 1000) <= 50)) AS hit
    FROM (SELECT 'size 1' AS name, xs FROM f1a UNION ALL SELECT 'size 0.2', xs FROM f1b),
         range(1001, 2001) r(t), LATERAL (SELECT cpt_pelt(xs[1:t], 'l2') AS b)
)
SELECT name, min(t) FILTER (WHERE hit) - 1000 AS first_alarm,
       coalesce(max(t) FILTER (WHERE NOT hit), 1000) + 1 - 1000 AS stable_from
FROM d GROUP BY name;
-- size 1     first alarm after 17 points, stable from 17
-- size 0.2   first alarm after 22 points, stable from 317
```

A change of one standard deviation is pinned down within 17 points and stays found. The 0.2 change
gets a lucky early alarm from a run of high values, which then disappears again. Only after about 300
points is there enough evidence for it to stay. This is the small-change problem the FOCuS simulations
measure. Rerunning PELT per point costs O(n) per point, which FOCuS avoids; use this to understand
delays, not as a production online detector.

## 2. Matt Fleming: change point detection on noisy benchmarks

Talk: "Using Change Point Detection to Fight Noisy Benchmark Results" (P99 CONF; slides on
SlideShare). Paper: Fleming et al., "Hunter: Using Change Point Detection to Hunt for Performance
Regressions", ICPE 2023, [arXiv:2301.03034](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.03034).

**What the talk is about.** Benchmark results are noisy because modern systems are nondeterministic.
"Eyeballing" graphs takes hours and is hard to teach. Thresholds are "hard to calculate" and "hard to
maintain". Change point detection works on the noisy series directly. Its drawbacks, from the slides:
it "needs multiple data points", there is "a 'delay' in when change points are identified", and the
"computational complexity can be prohibitive".

Hunter itself is E-divisive means with a Student's t-test in place of permutation tests (deterministic
and faster), p < 0.05 (usually), and a filter that drops changes below 5%. The paper's practical lessons
include using about 30 points rather than 14 (fewer false positives), and that "Change Point Detection
Cannot Fix Noisy Data": moving the benchmarks off noisy hardware stopped about 3 false positives a month.

### 2a. A noisy daily benchmark

The paper's main dataset has "175 entries and covers 15 months", with regressions and improvements,
including a regression that was reverted after 11 days. A synthetic series of that kind: 10,000 ops/s
with 3% noise, an 8% regression on days 60–70 that is then reverted, a 10% improvement from day 120,
and a 2% step from day 150.

```sql
CREATE TABLE bench AS
SELECT list(10000 * (CASE WHEN d BETWEEN 60 AND 70 THEN 0.92 WHEN d >= 150 THEN 1.10 * 1.02
                          WHEN d >= 120 THEN 1.10 ELSE 1.0 END)
            * (1 + 0.03 * z(d, 11)) ORDER BY d) AS xs
FROM range(175) t(d);
```

**Thresholds raise false alarms.** A 5% day-over-day rule fires 56 times in 175 days:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE abs(xs[k] / xs[k - 1] - 1) > 0.05) FROM bench, range(2, 176) r(k);   -- 56
```

**Scale before you penalise.** BIC assumes the cost is a −2 log-likelihood, which for `l2` means noise
with sd 1. On raw ops/s the noise sd is about 300, and `cpt_pelt(xs, 'l2')` returns 174 segments for
175 days. Divide by an estimate of the noise sd first. The median absolute deviation (MAD) of the
day-to-day differences, `mad(diff) · 1.4826 / √2`, is a standard estimate that is fairly robust to
the changes themselves:

```sql
CREATE MACRO noise_sd(xs) AS (
    SELECT mad(dx) * 1.4826 / sqrt(2)
    FROM (SELECT unnest(list_transform(range(2, len(xs) + 1), lambda k: xs[k] - xs[k - 1])) AS dx)
);

WITH s AS (SELECT xs, noise_sd(xs) AS sd FROM bench)
SELECT round(sd), cpt_pelt(list_transform(xs, lambda x: x / sd), 'l2') FROM s;
-- 380.0   [60, 71, 120, 149, 175]
```

The estimate (380) is somewhat above the true 300–330, because the level shifts leak into the
differences, which makes the penalty slightly conservative. The result is still exact: the regression
(days 61–71 in 1-based positions), its revert, the improvement, and the 2% step.

**Greedy search misses short regressions.** Binary segmentation first splits at the largest change and
never finds the 11-day dip:

```sql
WITH s AS (SELECT xs, noise_sd(xs) AS sd FROM bench)
SELECT cpt_binseg(list_transform(xs, lambda x: x / sd), 'l2') FROM s;      -- [120, 149, 175]
```

This is the same failure the paper reports for its permutation-based E-divisive on the reverted
regression ("only detected these changes for 15 of the 30 runs"). PELT is exact and does not have
this problem.

**Hunter's relative-change filter.** Drop change points whose segment mean changes by less than 5%:

```sql
WITH n AS (SELECT xs, noise_sd(xs) AS sd FROM bench),
s AS (SELECT xs, cpt_segment_stats(xs, cpt_pelt(list_transform(xs, lambda x: x / sd), 'l2')) AS segs FROM n)
SELECT list_append(
    list_transform(list_filter(range(1, len(segs)), lambda k: abs(segs[k + 1].mean / segs[k].mean - 1) >= 0.05),
                   lambda k: segs[k]."end"),
    len(xs))
FROM s;
-- [60, 71, 120, 175]
```

The measured changes are −7.6%, +8.3%, +8.6% (true +10%) and +3.1% (true +2%), so only the small step
is dropped. Note that estimated effects are noisy: with a true +6% improvement, this series measures
+4.7%, and a 5% filter would drop a real improvement. Choose the threshold well below the smallest
effect you care about.

### 2b. Latency with known change points

The paper's ground-truth experiment injects latency changes into a Cassandra cluster with Chaos Mesh
(9 scenarios: change in mean, in variance, or both) and scores detectors on p99 latency sampled every
second. In its Table 3, Hunter scored higher F1 than PELT and Dynp in every scenario. Those PELT and Dynp
runs used ruptures with the paper's own settings, so they say nothing about these algorithms in general.
For example, a cost that cannot see variance changes cannot find them, and an unscaled penalty
over-segments.

The same three kinds of change, 600 seconds at a p99 of about 20 ms:

```sql
CREATE TABLE latency AS
SELECT scenario, list(v ORDER BY i) AS xs FROM (
    SELECT 'mean' AS scenario, i, CASE WHEN i >= 300 THEN 30 ELSE 20 END + 2 * z(i, 21) AS v FROM range(600) t(i)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'variance', i, 20 + CASE WHEN i >= 300 THEN 6 ELSE 2 END * z(i, 21) FROM range(600) t(i)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'both', i, CASE WHEN i >= 200 THEN 25 ELSE 20 END + CASE WHEN i >= 400 THEN 6 ELSE 2 END * z(i, 21)
    FROM range(600) t(i)
) GROUP BY scenario;

SELECT scenario, cpt_pelt(xs, 'normal'), len(cpt_pelt(list_transform(xs, lambda x: x / 2), 'l2')) FROM latency;
-- both       [200, 400, 600]   55 segments with l2
-- mean       [300, 600]         2
-- variance   [300, 600]        80
```

The `normal` cost, which models both mean and variance, recovers every scenario exactly, with no
tuning. `l2`, even when scaled correctly for the quiet period, handles the mean change but breaks a
variance increase into dozens of spurious segments, because it reads the larger noise as level shifts.
Pick the cost that matches the kind of change you expect.

## Summary of the lessons

| Lesson | Source | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| Offline detection sees the whole series; online detection trades accuracy for delay | FOCuS Fig. 1, Fleming slide 21 | 1a, 1b |
| Small changes take far longer to confirm than to suspect | FOCuS simulations | 1b |
| Fixed thresholds raise false alarms on noisy data | Hunter §1, slides 11–13 | 2a |
| Penalties assume a noise scale; estimate it (MAD of differences) | changepoint docs, Hunter §5.3 | 2a |
| Greedy splitting can miss short, reverted regressions | Hunter §4.1 | 2a |
| A relative-change filter removes small, irrelevant shifts, but estimates are noisy | Hunter §3.4 | 2a |
| Match the cost to the change: mean, variance or both | Hunter §4.3 | 2b |
